text: By inverse scaling, I mean the opposite behavior shown in OpenAI's scaling laws (https://t.co/GVzMlmP07q) - that performance gets worse as model size, data size, and compute increase

author: EthanJPerez
text: Many of these problems will be solved in the next few years after scaling up model sizes. In the meanwhile, a good guide to choosing long-term important research problems is to ask: "Where will the LM objective actively teach the wrong behavior?"

author: EthanJPerez
text: Some say this is obvious - I agree. But this is the most compelling demo I've seen that the LM objective is flawed. NLP should focus much more on problems which show inverse scaling. Most of the focus rn is on problems that "should be hard" for LMs but don't show inverse scaling

author: EthanJPerez
text: I’m personally sad that true few-shot learning is so challenging, but I hope that you all will build on our findings to develop methods with real-world few-shot applications. We need them for low-resource languages and tasks that need expert annotation

author: EthanJPerez
text:
3. Submit your model for test evaluation directly, without first checking performance on validation.
4. Don’t rely on HPs from prior work that were tuned using validation for the same benchmark (e.g., SuperGLUE)

author: EthanJPerez
text:
Recommendations for future work:
1. Report all prompts/hyperparameters you considered and how you chose between them.
2. Include validation examples in the number of examples used by your method.

author: EthanJPerez
text: Overall, our findings suggest that prior work significantly overestimated the true few-shot ability of language models given the difficulty of few-shot prompt/hyperparameter selection.

author: EthanJPerez
text: It’s not just hard to choose prompts but hyperparameters too. Finetuning-based few-shot methods often choose training objectives+hyperparameters with held-out sets. ADAPET (SOTA on few-shot SuperGLUE) does much worse when choosing just two HPs in a true few-shot way.

author: EthanJPerez
text: We tried to choose better prompts in many different ways: varying the number of examples used, the amount of computation used, and the prompt selection criterion itself. We found similar results in all cases.

author: EthanJPerez
text: The marginal, average-case gains from prompt selection aren’t even reliable. For many tasks and training sets, few-shot prompt selection chooses prompts that do much worse than randomly-chosen prompts.

author: EthanJPerez
text: In other words, one reason that prompts are "worth so many examples" (https://t.co/HjcsCDccjj) is that they are often tuned on held-out examples.

author: EthanJPerez
text: We choose a prompt (out of several candidates) using only the given few-shot examples, with cross-validation (CV) or minimum description length (MDL). Both choose prompts that marginally outperform randomly-chosen ones and do much worse than prompts chosen with held-out sets.

author: EthanJPerez
text:
Language models are amazing few-shot learners with the right prompt, but how do we choose the right prompt? It turns out that people use large held-out sets(!). How do models like GPT3 do in a true few-shot setting?

We then evaluate if explanations are useful for recognizing textual entailment using the e-SNLI dataset. Both written explanations and decision-relevant keyword markings (“rationales”) are helpful, but rationales are more useful than explanations.

author: EthanJPerez
text:
Next, we examine a popular QA benchmark, HotpotQA, where prior work has disputed the value of decomposing a question into subquestions. We show that subquestions *are* helpful and expose how prior evaluation procedures underestimated the value of question decomposition.

author: EthanJPerez
text:
We use Rissanen Data Analysis (RDA) to provide insights on a variety of datasets. First, we verify that MDL reduces when we use a capability (asking and answering subquestions) that is known to be helpful on a carefully-controlled question-answering task (CLEVR).
4/N

author: EthanJPerez
text:
In our paper, we show how MDL addresses the empirical shortcomings of previous methods for analyzing datasets, we provide a theoretical argument justifying why MDL is the right measure to use.

We named our data analysis method after Jorma Rissanen, the father of MDL.
3/N

author: EthanJPerez
text:
We say a capability f(x) is useful if it reduces the length of the shortest program needed to perform a task (map x to y), as measured by Minimum Description Length (MDL). For example, if x is a question & y is an answer, then f(x) can be an oracle that answers subquestions.
